scenes.title: Where and when
narration: El vito is a traditional folk song, dance, and music genre of Andalusia with origins tracing back to the sixteenth century.
Its name alludes to Saint Vitus, the patron of dancers, and the lively dance associated with him.

Developed in the nineteenth century as a bolero-style dancing song, the tradition experienced a major mid-to-twentieth-century revival in Córdoba led by instructor Maruja Cazalla after it had fallen into local oblivion.
on_screen: Map: Spain · Europe
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: El vito is sung with lyrics that can be humorous or serious.

It has served multiple societal functions beyond folk dancing, including use as a political anthem during the Spanish Civil War ("El Quinto Regimiento") and controversially as a processional march for Holy Week in Córdoba.
Today it is a revived tradition.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The melody is played fast in a 3/8 time signature.
It utilizes the harmonic minor scale for ascending motives and the phrygian mode for descending motives, resulting in an harmonic accompaniment based on the Andalusian cadence.
Listen for the guitar, castanets.
The pulse is 3/8.
A fast-paced 3/8 melody featuring ascending harmonic minor scales and descending phrygian modes that resolve into a distinct Andalusian cadence, driven by energetic guitar and castanet accompaniment.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key historical and artistic figures include Maruja Cazalla, who revived the dance in Córdoba; her mentor Rita Fragero; composer Fernando J. Obradors; violinist Pablo de Sarasate; zarzuela composer Mariano Soriano Fuertes; jazz artists John Coltrane and Charlie Haden; and processional march composer Rafael Wals Dantas.
While broadly Andalusian in origin, El vito became specifically associated with Córdoba during the mid-to-late twentieth century following its local revival.
El vito is classified as a traditional folk dance and music genre of Andalusia, closely linked in its nineteenth-century development to the bolero form.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: El vito is variant of bolero: El vito was created in the nineteenth century as a dancing song typical of the bolero.
El vito is sibling of flamenco: Shares the phrygian mode and Andalusian cadence common to Andalusian musical traditions.

Rhythm pattern: Andalusian cadence based on harmonic minor ascending and phrygian descending motives. Instruments: guitar, castanets. Vocal style: sung with humorous or serious lyrics. Form: song and dance music. Mood: animated, fast, lively. It should sound like this: A fast-paced 3/8 melody featuring ascending harmonic minor scales and descending phrygian modes that resolve into a distinct Andalusian cadence, driven by energetic guitar and castanet accompaniment. New melody, new arrangement: do not quote or imitate any specific recorded song; keep the idiom, the instruments, the pulse and the proportions.

rules: Original composition only — no sampling, no melody of any existing recording, no lyrics from any song.
